prov.P_evidence: The final answer says "PyPI file lists checked by three researchers (no cp313t wheels for NumPy, pydantic-core or lxml; cp314t wheels for all three)". Report 3 did not check pydantic-core's file list; it says "A search summary says 2.34.1 still ships cp313t wheels, but I didn't open the file list to confirm." Report 1 also warned that "The PyPI pages were cut off at about 100k characters each." The answer drops both doubts and presents the wheel findings as settled agreement among all three researchers.

The final answer says "Turning Rosetta on is a fallback, but it has known hangs with Node (roadmap#384, for-mac#7075)" and presents the hangs as a current, settled problem. Report 1 says the GitHub issue "is from around Docker Desktop 4.24/4.25 and may be fixed now." Report 2 says "I don't know if Docker 4.26+ fully fixed the Rosetta/Node hangs. That claim is secondhand." Both reports attached that doubt, and the answer leaves it out.

The final answer says "Most uses are FFI (calls into C/C++) or SIMD, and the Foundation says so itself." Report 1 attributes only the FFI point to the Foundation ("notes that most uses are calls into C/C++ (FFI)"). Report 3 gets the SIMD point from a reviewer of Evans et al. ("A reviewer of Evans et al. notes that SIMD functions marked `unsafe` inflate the counts"), not from the Foundation.

The final answer says "With Rosetta the penalty is smaller. Independent tests put it at roughly 20–36%" and uses this for npm and Node work. Report 3 attached a doubt to those same figures: "I found no rigorous benchmark of Node under Docker Desktop Rosetta vs arm64. The figures above are sysbench runs or anecdotes." It also cited a report of amd64 running about 5–6× slower. The answer drops that caveat and states the 20–36% range as the settled Rosetta penalty.

The final answer states the 20.8% figure comes from "Cui et al., ICSE 2024, peer-reviewed" and says "Two independent registry-wide counts support it." Report 3 attributes the same 21,506/103,516 figure to "an arXiv preprint" (arXiv 2412.06251v1). The answer drops that doubt about peer review and presents the figure as settled. The answer also says "No count newer than May 2024 exists" and "Not verified: Nothing that would change the decision." All three reports only say they "found no 2025–2026 measurement," and Report 3 gives "moderate" confidence on the ~20% range. The answer turns that into "You can be confident in the ~20% range."

The final answer says the second NHANES analysis's "cardiovascular signal was mainly in older adults and was not significant in younger adults after full adjustment" and cites the PubMed record (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40944446/). That makes it look like a finding of the Aging Cell paper itself. Report 2 got this detail only from news-medical.net press coverage. Report 3 says it "couldn't read either full paper" and doesn't have "the cardiovascular hazard ratios from the Aging Cell study."

The final answer says "Rests on: ENTSO-E's and the Spanish government's own published findings, as read by Reports 1–3." Report 2 says "I could not open the ENTSO-E primary report" and Report 3 says "I did not open the ENTSO-E PDF itself." Both relied on trade-press summaries. The answer also cites ENTSO-E's own press release and report pages for "The panel says the oscillations did not directly cause the collapse, but the measures to damp them raised voltage. Data gaps left some trips unexplained." Reports 2 and 3 took those points from POWER magazine and pv-magazine, not from the ENTSO-E documents.

The final answer says "All three researchers independently found the following" and lists "Current releases of all three of your dependencies ship cp314t and cp315t wheels for Linux x86-64, but no cp313t: NumPy 2.5.4 ... pydantic-core 2.50.4 ...". Report 3 contradicts this: it lists under unsure "Whether the newest NumPy and pydantic-core releases still build cp313t wheels. I couldn't confirm either way." The answer also drops a doubt from Reports 1 and 2. Both said their PyPI fetches were cut off ("I can't fully rule out cp313t files further down"; "a cp313t wheel could be in the part I didn't see"), yet the answer states the absence of cp313t wheels as settled. Finally, the manylinux 2026-05-07 date is presented as an independent consensus, but every report cites the same PyTorch post. Report 2 notes "The manylinux date comes from PyTorch's post, not from manylinux's own changelog."

The final answer says "Its short-window group ate that way by circumstance, not deliberately" and "A short window often meant illness, poverty or skipped meals, not a planned 16:8 like yours." It presents this as settled, and the decision rests on it. Report 3 lists it as unresolved: "none of these studies separate people who fast on purpose from people who eat little because they're ill or poor." Reports 1 and 2 hedge it too: "often probably from irregular schedules," "Reverse causation is possible," and clinicians "point to confounders."

The final answer says "Every write would also block all readers across the network, which at 20 writes/s means latency and `SQLITE_BUSY` errors." Report 2 attached a doubt to this: "no source I found says rollback mode is reliable across hosts at about 20 writes/s. I found no benchmarks either. Lock round-trips, plus readers being blocked during every write, will probably cause SQLITE_BUSY errors and add latency." The answer drops that doubt and the 'probably', and states the outcome as settled.

The final answer says "About 1 in 5 crates (19.11%) use the `unsafe` keyword directly. This is 24,362 of the roughly 127,000 crates" and adds that "The 19.11% only works against the 'significant code' subset." That presents the figure as consistent with that denominator. Report 1 says "The arithmetic doesn't quite match either: 24,362 / 127,000 = 19.18%, while the post says 19.11%." Report 3 says "The arithmetic is slightly off: 24,362 / 127,000 = 19.18%, not 19.11%." The answer drops this mismatch. It also states "34.35% of crates directly call a crate that uses `unsafe`" without Report 1's caveat that "The 34.35% has no stated denominator."

The final answer says: "Rests on: ENTSO-E's own press release and the government and court publications, all read directly by our researchers." Report 1 contradicts this for the government source: "I did not read the Spanish government report or Portugal's own reviews (REN, ERSE) directly." None of the reports says the court publication was read directly either; Report 2 took the court closure from Vozpópuli press coverage. The answer also attributes "It was an overvoltage event, not a lack of inertia" to the ENTSO-E final report. The reports got that framing only from REE's own report and from press summaries such as Report 2's POWER/pv-tech sources and Report 3's Ars Technica, not from the ENTSO-E primary document.

The final answer states as settled: "Another observational analysis found the lowest risk at about 11–12 hour windows. It found no significant risk from short windows in younger adults after full adjustment." Report 3, the only source for this, says: "I haven't verified the details of the Mao 2025 study myself." Similarly, the answer says "Some trial data hint at small LDL rises" as the basis for a recommendation, while Report 1 says of that BMJ finding: "I only saw a snippet of that one and did not verify it."

The final answer says "Your dependencies have no current 3.13t wheels. The latest releases of NumPy (2.5.4) and lxml (6.1.3) ship cp314t wheels but no cp313t wheels" as settled, and the decision rests on it ("NumPy and lxml already rule 3.13t out"). Report 3 attached a doubt to this: "The PyPI pages were cut off when I read them. No cp313t wheels showed up in the parts I saw, but I couldn't fully rule them out (NumPy is the most likely to have some)." Report 1 also noted its NumPy and lxml JSON pages "were cut off before all files were read" and said it only "expect[s] those lists are complete." The answer drops both caveats.

The final answer says "It counts crates, not downloads, and popular crates use `unsafe` more often" as settled fact, and uses it to call 19% "a floor". The only basis in the reports is the Evans figure for popular crates (~60% or over 50%). Report 1 says "I couldn't extract the PDF text, so those last two numbers are unverified." Report 3 also says it "couldn't extract text from the PDF to confirm these breakdown numbers." The final answer even lists "the share of popular crates" under "Do not cite yet", yet it states the claim without that doubt.

The final answer states as settled that "Shift work and sleep were not accounted for" and that "The design flaws above stand without them" [the advocate researchers]. Both reports that looked for this said they could not check it. Report 1: "I couldn't read the full text to see which confounders were adjusted for." Report 3: "I couldn't read the full text of the 2025 paper or its covariate list." Report 2: "sleep and shift work weren't accounted for" came from the 34 researchers' letter, which Report 2 notes is from an interested party. The answer also states "31 of them died of cardiovascular causes" as fact, while Report 3 says "I couldn't get the exact number of cardiovascular deaths in the short-window group" and Report 1 says it couldn't see "the event counts in the final version."

The final answer states "Docker's Synchronized File Shares (4.27+, paid plan) ... https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/". This presents the paid-plan requirement as settled and cites it to the docs page. Report 1 says the requirement comes only from Docker's blog: "The docs page itself doesn't mention a subscription." It also lists under Uncertain: "I didn't confirm the subscription requirement for synchronized file shares on the docs page."

The final answer says "Rests on: ENTSO-E's own landing-page summary and the Government's published report" and cites the Government committee's findings to the lamoncloa full-report PDF. No report says the Government report was read. Report 3 says "I only read a press summary" and "I didn't read ... the full government report myself." Report 2 sourced it from balkangreenenergynews and pv-magazine. Report 1 only links the PDF and gives no sign of having read it. The answer also attributes the factual-report finding to the ENTSO-E landing page ("Same landing page"), but Report 1 got it from pv-tech coverage.

The final answer says "The SQLite docs warn that lock bugs on NFS have corrupted databases, sometimes silently and much later." The point about silent, delayed corruption comes only from Report 2, finding 3, which cites a SQLite forum post by a user ("NFS lied, so now the database is corrupt in some way that might or might not manifest"), not SQLite's official documentation. Reports 1 and 3 quote howtocorrupt.html and useovernet.html only on locks being buggy and corruption being possible. Report 3 adds that failures are "not frequent or repeatable," which is about how hard failures are to reproduce, not about silent corruption. Separately, "All three researchers traced this to SQLite's own docs" overstates Report 2, which got the WAL quote through GoToSocial's docs quoting SQLite, not from wal.html.

The final answer cites the full non-confidential PDF for the committee's findings: "insufficient voltage control (REE scheduled 10 synchronous units, one became unavailable, and some did not respond properly)… https://www.lamoncloa.gob.es/…Informe-no-confidencial-Comite-de-analisis-28A.pdf". No report says that PDF was read. Report 3 says of the committee: "I only read a press summary", and the 'one became unavailable' detail comes from press (Report 2: balkangreenenergynews/pv-magazine; Report 3: infobae). Likewise, "An industry-commissioned Comillas-IIT study calls it an inter-area mode" links the Comillas PDF as if it were the source. Report 3 says "The Comillas PDF wouldn't render, so its claims come from press coverage of it." The top-level caveat covers only the ENTSO-E report.

The final answer says "All three researchers found this in the abstract and coverage" about the one-day recall measurement. Report 2 says "PubMed and ScienceDirect were blocked" and drew this detail from AHA news and STAT coverage, not the paper's abstract. Report 1's sources for it were also press coverage (news-medical, mdedge, Attia, ScienceFocus). So the claim that all three got it from the study's abstract overstates the provenance.

The final answer says "The researchers read the PyPI file lists for the latest releases of all three of your dependencies... none ship cp313t" and lists "the current PyPI file lists... read by the researchers" under "Rests on", stated as settled. Report 1 says "The PyPI pages were cut off at about 100k characters each. The cp313 wheels I could see were all the normal GIL builds." Report 3 says it "didn't open the file list to confirm" for pydantic-core, and a summary it saw claimed cp313t wheels still shipped. The answer also turns the reports' "I found no official statement" on lxml thread safety into "lxml has published nothing on thread safety."

Final answer: "In one 16:8 trial it did no better than the control group, and much of the weight lost was muscle." Report 3 qualifies the lean-mass finding: "That came from a subset of only 50 people." The answer drops that caveat and states the muscle-loss finding as settled.

The final answer states as settled: "NumPy 2.5.4 and lxml 6.1.3 ship cp314t wheels but no cp313t ones." It attaches the truncation caveat only to pydantic-core. Report 3 says: "The PyPI pages were cut off when I read them. No cp313t wheels showed up in the parts I saw, but I couldn't fully rule them out (NumPy is the most likely to have some)." Report 1 also notes that the lxml and NumPy JSON pages were cut off before all files were read.

The final answer says "Update Docker Desktop, and move from node:20 ... to node:22. Both fixed npm-install hangs under amd64 emulation." This states the fix as settled. Report 3 hedged it: "Docker Desktop 4.26 reportedly fixed the Rosetta freeze, but QEMU reports continued into 2025." Report 2 listed the upgrades only as workarounds users tried in an issue thread, not as confirmed fixes.

The final answer says: "Rests on: The study's design, read in the AHA release and the paper's abstract: two-day recall, small confounded group, no all-cause signal, authors disclaim causation." But Report 1 gives the two-recall measurement, the 414-person group, the 31 deaths and the smoker/BMI/demographic confounding only in its point 3, which cites TCTMD press coverage (https://www.tctmd.com/news/...). Its summaries of the AHA release (point 1) and the abstract (point 2) contain none of these details. Report 2 also sources them to TCTMD and the advocates' letter. Reports 2 and 3 say they could not open the paper. So these details came from press coverage and critics, not from the primary sources the answer says they were read in.

The final answer says: "CNMC (Apr 2026). It opened sanction proceedings and says these do not assign cause. https://www.cnmc.es/prensa/informe-incidente-electrico-20260319". This presents the sanction proceedings, and the CNMC's statement that they do not assign cause, as coming from the CNMC's own page. In Report 1, that CNMC link is the 19 March 2026 recommendations report, which 'names no cause'. Report 1 got the sanction cases and the 'do not attribute the cause' statement from eldiario.es. Report 3 got them from infobae and Report 2 from elindependiente. All three are press coverage, not the CNMC primary source.
